levels.title: When I was a child…
levels.full: Using Would to Express a Repeated Action in the Past

items.title: would = again and again, long ago
lines: A repeated action in the past.
Same meaning as used to.

When I was a child, my father used to read me a story at night.

items.title: Action or state?

examples.text: I would build sandcastles at the beach.
I used to build sandcastles at the beach.
I used to live in California.
He used to be a Boy Scout.
They used to have a Ford.

items.tip: States: be, live, have, know, like. ❌ They would have a Ford.

items.text: They ___ live in the city, but when I was ten, they moved to the coast.

items.text: Every summer, I ___ visit my grandparents. (repeated action)

lines: would + verb = a repeated past action (= used to).

talk.title: My childhood
talk.task: Tell Claude 5 things about your childhood with “I used to…” and “I would…”.
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. Ask me about my childhood, one question at a time: Where did you use to live? What were you like as a child? What would you do every summer? What would you do after school? What did you use to be afraid of? I answer with used to for past states (be, live, have, like) and would or used to for repeated actions. levels.title: Should have…
levels.full: Expressing the Past: Necessity, Advisability, Expectation

items.title: The past is had to
lines: Only one past form for necessity.
chips: Julia has to get a visa. → Julia had to get a visa.
must get → had to get
has got to get → had to get
items.tip: ❌ Sorry I'm late. I must drop my mom off. ✅ I had to drop my mom off.

items.text: Sorry I'm late. I ___ drop my mom off at the mall.

items.title: should have = a mistake
lines: should have + past participle.
It was a good idea, but I didn't do it.

examples.text: I failed the test. I should have studied for it.
I shouldn't have gone to the movies the night before.

items.text: “I should have studied.” Did the speaker study?

items.title: was supposed to = it didn't happen
lines: A plan or duty that failed.
chips: We are supposed to leave now.
We were supposed to leave last week. (but we didn't)

items.title: should have = I expected it
lines: It was expected by now.
chips: The mail should be here.
The mail should have been here by now.

items.text: “We were supposed to have a party last weekend.” What happened?
items.why: was / were supposed to = it didn't happen.

lines: Past necessity: had to. Past advice: should have + past participle (but I didn't).
was / were supposed to: an expectation that didn't happen.

examples.text: Julia had to get a visa.

items.text: How was your weekend?
options: Not fun. I had to clean my house.

items.why: Past of have to → had to.

Do you have to retake the test? → ___ the test this morning?
When do we have to register to vote? → When ___ to vote for this election?

talk.title: What should Tom have done?

She took his paper, failed him, and the school suspended him for a week. Ask me: What should or shouldn't Tom have done? What should or shouldn't the teacher have done? What should or shouldn't the school have done? Check that I use should(n't) have + past participle.

lesson.title: Learn: must be, may be, might be

items.title: Three levels of sure
lines: A fact needs no modal.
must = I'm almost sure. may / might / could = maybe.

items.title: must = my best guess
lines: I have a good reason. I can't think of another answer.
chips: Nadine has missed a week of class. She must be really sick.

examples.text: Why isn't John in class? He must be sick.

items.title: Maybe: may, might, could
lines: I don't really know.
chips: He may be sick.
He might be at the library.
He could be out of town.
items.tip: maybe (one word) = perhaps: Maybe he is sick. may be (two words) = a verb: He may be sick.

items.text: Alice always gets the best grades in the class. She ___ study hard.
items.why: A strong reason → my best guess: must.

items.text: Where's Ms. Adams? — I don't know. She ___ be at a meeting, or maybe she's in the lounge.
items.why: I don't know. One idea of two → may.

items.title: Not can!
lines: can is not for guessing.
chips: ❌ He can be sick.
✅ He could be sick.
✅ He may be sick.

lines: 100%: He is sick. 95%: He must be sick. 50% or less: He may / might / could be sick.

talk.title: Why? Make a guess
talk.task: Claude describes someone. You guess why with “must”: “She must be cold.”
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. Describe one situation at a time and ask Why?: Carol has goose bumps on her arms. / Bob is scratching his arm. / Yusef is staring off into space. / Katrina is blushing. / The baby is crying. / My neighbor is carrying a suitcase. I make a logical guess with must (She must be cold.). Sometimes ask me something I can't know (What do I have in my bag?) so that I answer with 'I don't know. It may / might / could be ...'. Check the forms.

levels.title: It can't be true!
levels.full: Degrees of Certainty: Present Time Negative

lesson.title: Learn: can't be, must not be, may not be

items.title: Four levels of “no”
lines: can't / couldn't = impossible!
must not = probably not. may not / might not = maybe not.

items.title: Impossible, or my best guess?

left.label: can't / couldn't: I don't believe it

examples.text: Sam can't be hungry. I just saw him eat a huge meal.
Sam isn't eating his food. He must not be hungry.

items.tip: may not / might not: just one possibility. Maybe he doesn't feel well.

items.text: Ryan ___ be a doctor! He failed all his exams.
Rosa doesn't want water, coffee, or a soft drink. She ___ be thirsty.
Daniel hasn't answered my text. He ___ have his phone with him. I'm not sure.

lines: can't / couldn't be = impossible. must not be = probably not.
may not / might not be = maybe not.

examples.text: Sam can't be hungry. He just ate.
He must not be hungry.
He may not be hungry.

items.text: Rob says, “That isn't true.”
items.ctx: Someone said Ed quit his job and moved to a Pacific island.

items.text: Hamid says, “That can't be true.”
Lucy says, “That may not be true.”
Linda says, “That must not be true.”
Someone left this jacket here. I think it belongs to Alex. — It couldn't belong to him.
options: He never wears jackets like that. It's much too small.

items.text: Someone told me that Karen is in Norway. — She couldn't be in Norway.
options: I just saw her five minutes ago.
items.why: A strong reason why it's impossible.

items.text: Look at that animal. Is it a wolf? — It couldn't be a wolf.
options: There are no wolves in this country.
items.why: A strong reason why it's impossible.

items.text: Yuko has flunked every test so far. She (95% sure) ___ very hard.

talk.title: The power is out
talk.task: The lights go out at home, with no wind. Talk with Claude about what may, must or couldn't be the cause.
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. Role-play: we are at home in the evening and the power suddenly goes out. The weather is calm. Start by sounding a little afraid and ask 'What could it be?'. I make guesses with may / might / could be, reject ideas with couldn't be or can't be (and give a reason), and reach a logical conclusion with must be. Offer your own ideas too. Check my modals of certainty.

items.title: Guess about the past
lines: modal + have + past participle.
chips: She was sick. (100%)
She must have been sick. (95%)
She may / might / could have been sick. (50% or less)

items.text: Why wasn't Mary in class? I saw her yesterday and she looked ill. She ___ sick.
items.why: A sure guess about the past → must have been.

items.title: Negative guesses about the past
lines: Same ladder, with not.
chips: Sam wasn't hungry. (100%)
Sam couldn't have been hungry. (impossible)
Sam must not have been hungry. (95%)
Sam may not / might not have been hungry. (50%)

items.text: He looked at everything on the table and saw no sunglasses. “You ___ them there.”
items.why: He thinks it's impossible → couldn't have left.

items.title: The form never changes
lines: have, not has. Then the past participle.
chips: ✅ It may have fallen out of my purse.
❌ It may have fell out.
❌ She must has been sick.

items.text: I can't find my wallet. It may have ___ out of my purse.

lines: Past guess: must / may / might / could + have + past participle.
Impossible in the past: couldn't have / can't have + past participle.

examples.text: She must have been sick.
She might have been sick.
Sam couldn't have been hungry.

items.text: Laura thinks it's possible, but she's just guessing: “You ___ them on the table at the restaurant.”

Maya remembers seeing them on the table: “You ___ them there. That's the only explanation.”
items.why: The only explanation → must have left.

items.text: The doorbell rang while I was napping. Maybe it was a friend. → It ___ a friend.
items.why: Maybe, in the past → might have been.

items.text: It's not possible that it was my next-door neighbor. He was at work. → It ___ my neighbor.
items.why: Impossible, in the past → couldn't have been.

items.text: There was a package outside my door. I'm 95% sure it was a delivery person. → It ___ a delivery person.
items.why: 95% sure, in the past → must have been.

items.text: My friend never thanked me for the present. I believe she ___ it.
items.why: A logical guess, negative → must not have gotten.

items.text: My mother thinks it ___ lost in the mail, but she's just guessing.
Dan had a huge argument with his girlfriend last night.

Dick is going to wait to get married until he has a better job.
options: It must not have been Dick.
items.why: He wants to wait → probably not.

items.text: Doug isn't sure he's ready. He thinks he's a little young.
options: It may not have been Doug.
items.why: Not sure → may not have been.

items.text: Larry was absent yesterday afternoon. — I don't know. He ___ class.
items.why: I don't know, past → might have skipped.

items.text: I don't think so. He's not the type. — Then he ___ an appointment.
items.why: A stronger guess → must have had.

items.text: I can't find my wallet. It may have fell out of my purse.
items.fix: I can't find my wallet. It may have fallen out of my purse.

items.text: Paula fell asleep in class this morning. She ___ too late last night.
items.why: A sure guess about last night.

items.text: Marco had to give a speech in front of 500 people. He ___ nervous.
items.why: A sure guess about the past.

items.text: You walked into a door? Ouch! That ___.

items.say: You could have told them what you planned to do.

talk.title: What happened?
talk.task: Claude asks why something happened. Guess first with might have, then with must have.
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. Ask me one question at a time: Beth seems upset. What happened? / How did Claudio get to school today? / The subway station is closed. Why? / Larry was absent yesterday afternoon. Where was he? I answer with a weak guess (She may / might / could have ...). Then you disagree ('I don't think so, because ...') and I make a stronger conclusion with must have. Check the form: modal + have + past participle.

lesson.title: Learn: will, should, may / might / could

items.title: Three levels for the future
lines: will = 100%. should / ought to = 90%. may / might / could = 50%.
chips: Kay will do well on the test. (I'm sure)
Kay should do well on the test. (almost sure)
Kay ought to do well on the test.
She may / might / could do well. (I'm guessing)

items.text: You've trained for months for the race. You ___ do really well. (almost sure)
items.why: Almost sure about the future → should.

items.title: must vs. should

examples.text: Lots of people are in line for that movie. It must be good.
She isn't here now, but she should be home around nine.

items.tip: A promise? Use will: I will be there at seven.

items.text: Jack's car is in front of his house. He ___ be at home.
We're almost ready to eat. The rice ___ be done in five minutes.

lines: Future: will (100%), should / ought to (90%), may / might / could (50%).
must = a sure guess about now, not the future.

talk.title: Distracted drivers

talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. talk.title: The mystery couple

talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. Read me this scene: MAN: I don't think you should do this alone. WOMAN: But you don't understand. I have to. MAN: Let me go with you. WOMAN: No, I'll be fine. MAN: You must let me help. WOMAN: There's nothing you can do. This is something I need to do for myself. (She leaves.) Then ask me one question at a time: Where are they?
